📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — what the OS did in the last second

WORKED EXAMPLE — one keystroke, every OS role
You press a key in a text editor while music plays:
1. The keyboard raises an interrupt; the OS’s handler reads the character (device management).
2. The scheduler decides the editor process should run next; a context switch restores its registers (CPU management).
3. The editor’s pages are already in RAM — the MMU translates its virtual addresses (memory management).
4. Autosave writes via the file system (storage management), and the music process keeps getting its CPU slices throughout (fair multiplexing).
One second of “nothing” = thousands of these decisions. The OS is a resource manager (divide CPU/RAM/disk among processes) and an abstraction layer (files instead of disk blocks, processes instead of timeslices).
⚠️ KERNEL MODE vs USER MODE
The hardware enforces two privilege levels: the kernel runs privileged instructions (I/O, page tables); user programs must ASK via system calls. That boundary is the answer to half the intro questions.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

An operating system is the layer that turns raw hardware into something usable. Every program you run, every file you save, every network packet you send — they all pass through the OS. Knowing what the OS actually does, and where it fits in the stack, is the prerequisite to understanding everything else in this course.

Core concepts

1. Two essential roles. First, abstraction: the OS hides messy hardware behind clean interfaces. A file is simpler than disk sectors; a process is simpler than CPU registers; a socket is simpler than network frames. Second, resource management: the OS shares finite hardware (CPU, memory, disk, network) safely among many programs that don't trust each other.

2. User mode and kernel mode. Modern CPUs have privilege rings. User-mode code (your program) cannot directly touch hardware or other processes' memory. Kernel-mode code (the OS) can. The transition between them is controlled — through system calls, interrupts, and exceptions. This separation is the security and stability foundation of multiuser systems.

3. The kernel — the OS proper. Process scheduling, memory management, file systems, device drivers, networking — all live in the kernel. Userspace tools (shell, file utilities, applications) call into the kernel through system calls. Different OSes draw the kernel boundary differently; the role is the same.

4. Major OS families. Unix-like (Linux, macOS, BSD) — descended from a 1970s research OS, dominant on servers and mobile. Windows NT family — designed independently, dominant on desktops and enterprise. Real-time OSes (VxWorks, FreeRTOS) — for hard timing constraints. Mobile (Android, iOS) — Unix kernels with custom userspace.

5. What 'the OS' includes — and excludes. Strictly: the kernel. Loosely: kernel plus standard libraries, shells, utilities. Even more loosely: the whole 'system' a user sees, including window manager and apps. When someone says 'OS,' check which scope they mean.

6. Multiprogramming and time-sharing. Early computers ran one program at a time. Multiprogramming keeps the CPU busy by overlapping I/O of one process with computation of another. Time-sharing extends this to interactive use — many users share one machine via fast context switches. These ideas now run inside every laptop and phone.

7. Why OS internals still matter. Cloud, containers, and managed runtimes hide the OS — but only when things work. Performance debugging, security incidents, reliability tuning all eventually demand kernel-level reasoning. An engineer who treats the OS as a black box stops growing past a certain seniority.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Conflating 'the OS' with 'the kernel' — both meanings exist; clarify which.
  • Assuming user-mode and kernel-mode is just a permission check — it is hardware-enforced through CPU privilege rings.
  • Treating Linux, macOS, and Windows as interchangeable — POSIX similarities are real, but kernel internals differ deeply.
  • Believing managed languages or containers eliminate the need to understand the OS — they just defer it to crisis time.

Quick recap

An OS abstracts hardware and manages shared resources. The kernel runs in privileged mode; user programs run in user mode and request services via system calls. Multiprogramming and time-sharing keep hardware busy and many users productive. Major OS families share core ideas but differ in implementation.

Glossary

Operating system
Software layer between hardware and applications, providing abstraction and resource management.
Kernel
The core OS running in privileged mode with full hardware access.
User mode / kernel mode
Hardware-enforced CPU privilege levels separating applications from OS code.
Multiprogramming
Keeping the CPU busy by overlapping I/O and computation across several processes.
Time-sharing
Multiple users sharing one machine through rapid context switches.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — a system call, traced across the boundary

WORKED EXAMPLE — what printf() really does
printf("hi")                 ← user code, user mode
  → C library formats text
  → write(1, "hi", 2)        ← the SYSTEM CALL
     → TRAP instruction: CPU switches to KERNEL mode
     → kernel validates fd 1, copies the bytes, drives the device
     → returns 2 (bytes written); CPU drops back to USER mode
The trap is the ONLY door into the kernel: a controlled jump to a fixed handler, with arguments checked before anything privileged happens. fork/exec/read/write/open all cross this same doorway.
⚠️ SYSTEM CALL ≠ FUNCTION CALL
A function call stays in user mode (nanoseconds). A system call changes privilege mode via trap (much costlier) — which is why buffered I/O batches many prints into one write. “Which requires a mode switch?” is the exam’s favorite.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Every interaction with the OS — opening a file, allocating memory, creating a process, sending a packet — happens through a system call. They are the API of the kernel. Understanding what a system call costs, how it works, and which categories exist is what lets you reason about performance, debugging, and security.

Core concepts

1. What a system call is. A controlled transition from user mode to kernel mode. The user program sets up arguments, executes a special instruction (syscall, int 0x80, svc), and the CPU jumps to a kernel-defined handler. The kernel validates inputs, performs the work, places the result in a register, and returns. Hardware-enforced and centralized.

2. The cost of a system call. Crossing the user/kernel boundary is much more expensive than a normal function call — roughly 100-1000 ns on modern CPUs. Cache lines flush, TLB entries may invalidate, registers save and restore. Hot loops issuing millions of small system calls are a classic performance killer; batching is the standard fix.

3. The major system call categories. Process control (fork, exec, exit, waitpid). File management (open, read, write, close, lseek). Device management (ioctl, mmap). Information maintenance (gettimeofday, getpid, sysctl). Communication (pipe, socket, send, recv). Protection (chmod, setuid). Memorize the categories; the specific names you can look up.

4. The C library wraps most syscalls. When you call printf or malloc, you're calling C library functions that may eventually invoke a system call. The C library provides convenience and buffering. read() in C maps almost directly to the read syscall; printf buffers internally before calling write. Knowing where the boundary sits matters for debugging.

5. Errors and errno. Most system calls return -1 on error and set the global errno (or thread-local equivalent). Always check return values. errno gives a numeric code; strerror or perror translates to human-readable text. Modern languages wrap this in exceptions, but the underlying pattern is universal.

6. Tracing system calls. strace (Linux), dtruss (macOS), Process Monitor (Windows) record every system call a process makes. Invaluable for debugging 'why is this slow?', 'what file is it trying to open?', 'why is it failing?'. Master one of these tools — the visibility it provides is unmatched.

7. Direct calls vs library wrappers. Calling syscalls directly (assembly, syscall(2) function) is rare; library wrappers handle errno, ABI quirks, and platform differences. Some performance-critical or specialized code (sandboxes, debuggers, init systems) does call directly.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Issuing millions of single-byte read/write syscalls — performance disaster; batch into larger buffers.
  • Ignoring return values — failed system calls silently corrupt program state.
  • Confusing C library function calls (printf, malloc) with system calls — they are not always the same.
  • Reading errno without immediately calling strerror or perror — later code may overwrite it.

Quick recap

System calls are the kernel's API: a hardware-mediated transition from user to kernel mode. They are expensive compared to function calls; batch where possible. Categories cover process control, files, devices, info, communication, protection. The C library wraps most calls; tracing tools expose them. Always check return values and errno.

Glossary

System call
A controlled user-to-kernel transition for requesting OS services.
User-kernel boundary
Hardware-enforced separation requiring system calls to cross.
errno
Global (or thread-local) variable holding the last system call's error code.
strace / dtruss
Tools recording every system call a process makes.
C library wrapper
Function in libc translating an API call into one or more system calls.

System call: the programmatic way a program requests an OS service — opening files, allocating memory, creating processes. It crosses from user mode into the kernel, which validates and performs the privileged work.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

📖 Worked example — monolithic vs microkernel vs layers

WORKED EXAMPLE — the same crash, three architectures
A file-system bug hits:
• Monolithic (Linux): FS code runs IN the kernel → the whole system can panic. But calls between components are fast function calls.
• Microkernel (Minix, QNX): FS runs as a user-space server → it crashes ALONE and restarts; the kernel keeps only IPC/scheduling/memory. Cost: every service request is message-passing (slower).
• Layered/modular: Linux’s loadable kernel modules give some middle ground — drivers load/unload at runtime, but still run privileged.
Trade = performance (monolithic) vs isolation/reliability (microkernel). Virtual machines add another layer: a hypervisor multiplexing whole OSes.
⚠️ MATCH THE PROPERTY TO THE DESIGN
“Smallest possible kernel, services in user space” → microkernel. “Best raw performance, single privileged blob” → monolithic. “Drivers loadable at runtime” → modular. The exam gives the property, you name the architecture.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Where do you draw the boundary between kernel and user space? Different OS architectures answer differently — monolithic, microkernel, hybrid, exokernel. Each tradeoff (performance vs modularity vs reliability) shapes the OS for decades. Knowing which architecture an OS uses helps explain its design choices and limits.

Core concepts

1. Monolithic kernels. Everything kernel-mode lives in one large kernel binary: schedulers, drivers, file systems, networking. Linux is the canonical example. Fast (no boundary crossing between subsystems) but less isolated — a faulty driver can crash the whole kernel.

2. Microkernels. Only the bare minimum lives in kernel mode: scheduling, memory management, IPC. File systems, drivers, networking run in user-mode servers and communicate via message passing. Mach, MINIX, QNX. More isolated and modular; slower because every subsystem call is an IPC.

3. Hybrid kernels. Pragmatic middle ground. Windows NT and macOS XNU borrow microkernel ideas but keep performance-critical pieces in the kernel. Definition is fuzzy; some say 'monolithic with tendencies' rather than a distinct architecture.

4. Layered systems. OS organized in strict layers, each using only the one below. Clean conceptual model; rarely strict in practice because cross-layer optimizations matter for performance.

5. Exokernels and unikernels. Exokernel: minimal kernel exposing hardware safely; libraries in user space implement abstractions. Unikernel: a single application linked with a library OS, deployed as one bootable image. Niche but growing in cloud and edge.

6. Loadable kernel modules. Even monolithic kernels have escape valves. Linux kernel modules can be loaded/unloaded at runtime — drivers, file systems, security modules. Best of both worlds: monolithic performance, modular development. Moduality without microkernel cost.

7. Why architecture choice matters today. Most ground-truth performance numbers favor monolithic. Most security and reliability research favors microkernels. Most production deployments use hybrid. The pragmatic answer is rarely architecturally pure; it's whatever balances enough of each axis for the workload.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Calling Linux a 'pure monolith' — modules and namespaces blur the picture.
  • Calling macOS a 'microkernel' because XNU is Mach-based — most subsystems run kernel-mode.
  • Assuming microkernel = slow — message-passing optimizations narrow the gap considerably.
  • Treating architecture choice as religious — it is engineering tradeoff, not identity.

Quick recap

Monolithic: everything kernel-side, fast, less isolated. Microkernel: minimum kernel, services in user space, isolated, slower. Hybrid: practical middle. Layered: clean model, often impure in practice. Loadable modules give monolithic kernels modularity at runtime. Production OSes pick the tradeoff their workload needs.

Glossary

Monolithic kernel
Kernel containing all major OS subsystems in one privileged binary.
Microkernel
Minimal kernel with most subsystems running as user-mode servers.
Hybrid kernel
Architecture combining monolithic performance with some microkernel modularity.
Kernel module
Loadable code added to a running kernel without reboot.
Unikernel
Single-purpose OS with one application linked with a library OS as one image.

📘 Deep dive: hypervisors & systemd

Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor runs directly on hardware (ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM) — datacenter standard, best performance. Type 2 (hosted) runs as an application on a normal OS (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation) — convenient for desktops. systemd is the init system and service manager on modern Linux: PID 1, it boots the system, starts and supervises services (systemctl start/enable/status), and manages dependencies between them.

Containers vs VMs: containers share the host kernel, giving lightweight isolation with near-instant startup; VMs virtualize entire machines. Open source exposes its code for inspection and modification (Linux); closed source does not (Windows) — the accurate distinction is code availability, not price or quality.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A process is the OS's representation of a running program. Every command you type, every server that runs, every browser tab is one. Understanding the process model — its lifecycle, its memory layout, the system calls that create and end it — is foundational to everything that runs above the OS.

Core concepts

1. What a process actually is. A program is a passive file; a process is the active execution of that program. The OS represents each process with a Process Control Block (PCB) — a struct holding the program counter, registers, memory layout, open files, scheduling state, parent and children, and credentials.

2. Process memory layout. Each process gets its own virtual address space, typically segmented as: text (code), data (initialized globals), bss (uninitialized globals), heap (grows up via malloc), stack (grows down per thread). Memory mappings (mmap), shared libraries, and kernel-reserved regions fill the rest.

3. Process states. New (being created) → Ready (waiting for CPU) → Running (currently on CPU) → Blocked/Waiting (sleeping for I/O) → Terminated. Transitions happen on events: scheduler picks ready, I/O completes, syscall blocks. Understanding the state machine explains performance behavior.

4. fork and exec — the Unix model. fork() creates a near-copy of the calling process; both parent and child continue from the fork call. exec() replaces the current process image with a new program. Together they implement 'launch a program': fork, then have the child exec the new program. Strange-feeling but extremely flexible.

5. Process termination. exit(status) — voluntary. Receiving an unhandled fatal signal — involuntary. The parent process collects exit status with wait/waitpid. A child whose parent never waits becomes a zombie; one whose parent dies first becomes orphaned and re-parented to init.

6. The init process. PID 1 — the first process the kernel starts. All other processes descend from it. Modern Linux uses systemd or similar; older systems used SysV init. Special role: re-parents orphans, handles system shutdown, must never die.

7. Process vs program vs job. Program: file on disk. Process: active execution. Job: shell-level grouping (foreground/background). One program may have many simultaneous processes; one process may be one job or part of a pipeline.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Confusing fork and exec — fork copies; exec replaces. The combination is what 'launches' programs.
  • Forgetting wait() — leaves zombies that consume PCB slots.
  • Assuming child shares memory with parent post-fork — they have separate address spaces (copy-on-write under the hood, but logically separate).
  • Treating exit code 0 as 'optional' — shells and scripts depend on it for error chaining.

Quick recap

A process is an executing program with its own address space, register state, and OS bookkeeping (PCB). Memory divides into text/data/bss/heap/stack. State machine: new → ready → running → blocked → terminated. fork+exec creates new processes. wait reaps children; init re-parents orphans. The process model underlies every OS service.

Glossary

Process
An executing instance of a program with its own address space and OS state.
PCB (Process Control Block)
Kernel data structure tracking a process's state, registers, memory, and resources.
fork()
System call creating a near-duplicate of the calling process.
exec()
System call replacing the current process's program with a new one.
Zombie process
Terminated process whose parent has not yet collected its exit status.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — scheduling algorithms, computed

WORKED EXAMPLE — RR vs SJF on the same jobs
Jobs at t=0: P1=6, P2=3, P3=1 (ms).
SJF: order P3, P2, P1 → waits: P3=0, P2=1, P1=4 → avg 1.67.
Round-robin, quantum 2: P1(0-2) P2(2-4) P3(4-5) P1(5-7) P2(7-8) P1(8-10).
Waits: P3=4, P2=(2)+(7-4)=5, P1=(5-2)+(8-7)=4 → avg 4.33.
SJF minimizes average waiting (provably optimal) but needs burst predictions and can starve long jobs; RR guarantees responsiveness (nobody waits more than (n−1)×quantum for a turn) at the cost of switches. Preemptive priority + aging is the practical compromise real OSes use.
⚠️ QUANTUM SIZE IS A DIAL
Huge quantum → RR degrades into FCFS. Tiny quantum → context-switch overhead eats the CPU. “What happens as the quantum grows/shrinks?” is a guaranteed question.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

There are always more ready processes than CPUs. The scheduler decides who runs next, for how long, and in what order. Its choices determine whether your system feels snappy or sluggish, whether throughput is high or low, whether real-time deadlines are met. Every OS course studies scheduling because every OS does it.

Core concepts

1. Scheduling goals — they conflict. Throughput (work done per second). Latency / response time (how fast a single request completes). Fairness (each process gets a fair share). Predictability (deadlines met). Energy (mobile / cloud cost). No single algorithm wins all goals; production schedulers balance them.

2. Preemptive vs non-preemptive. Preemptive: scheduler can interrupt a running process at any time. Non-preemptive (cooperative): a process keeps the CPU until it voluntarily yields or blocks. Modern general-purpose OSes are preemptive; some embedded and real-time systems are cooperative.

3. FCFS (First-Come, First-Served). Simplest. The convoy effect bites: one slow process delays everyone behind it. Average wait time can be terrible. Educational; rarely used directly in production.

4. SJF (Shortest Job First). Provably optimal for average wait time — but requires knowing job length in advance. Approximated in practice with predictions based on past behavior. Long jobs may starve. Preemptive variant: SRTF (Shortest Remaining Time First).

5. Round Robin. Each process gets a fixed time quantum, then goes to the back of the ready queue. Simple, fair, responsive. Quantum size is critical: too short and overhead dominates, too long and it degrades to FCFS. Typical: 10-100 ms.

6. Priority and Multilevel Feedback Queue. Each process has a priority; scheduler picks highest. Pure priority risks starvation; aging (gradually raising priority of waiting processes) prevents it. MLFQ uses several queues at different priorities, demoting CPU-bound jobs and promoting I/O-bound ones — captures the instinct that interactive tasks should respond fast.

7. Linux's CFS — Completely Fair Scheduler. Tracks per-process virtual runtime; always picks the process with the smallest. Effectively a Weighted Fair Queueing scheduler in red-black tree form. Supplanted by EEVDF in newer kernels. Fair, low-overhead, multi-core aware.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Optimizing for one metric (throughput) and watching another collapse (interactivity).
  • Choosing a Round Robin quantum without measuring — defaults are educated guesses.
  • Implementing pure priority without aging — long-running low-priority work never finishes.
  • Treating all I/O the same — a fast SSD I/O burst differs from a network round-trip in scheduling implications.

Quick recap

Scheduling chooses which ready process runs next. Goals (throughput, latency, fairness, predictability) conflict. Algorithms range from FCFS (simple, unfair) to MLFQ (adaptive, complex) to CFS (fair-share). Real systems use sophisticated multi-queue designs. Quantum size, priority, aging, and I/O-vs-CPU detection all matter.

Glossary

Scheduler
OS component selecting the next process to run on a CPU.
Preemption
Interrupting a running process to run another.
Time quantum
Maximum CPU time a process holds before scheduler reconsiders.
Starvation
Indefinite postponement of a process due to scheduling policy.
Aging
Gradual priority raise for waiting processes to prevent starvation.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — threads vs processes, concretely

WORKED EXAMPLE — a web server’s choice
Serving 1,000 simultaneous connections:
• Process per connection: each has its own address space — bulletproof isolation, but fork + per-process memory + heavyweight context switches.
• Thread per connection: all share ONE address space (code, heap, open files), each having only its own stack + registers — cheap to create, cheap to switch, and they can share a cache in memory directly.
The cost of sharing: two threads touching the same counter race (ch3’s whole topic). A crash in one thread can take down the whole process — the isolation you gave up.
⚠️ WHAT’S SHARED vs PRIVATE
Shared: code, globals/heap, open file descriptors. Private per thread: stack, registers, program counter. Exams ask exactly this split — memorize the two lists.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Threads are the OS's answer to 'cheaper than processes, but still concurrent.' Multiple threads share one address space — they can communicate through memory rather than IPC. They unlock CPU parallelism and I/O concurrency for a single program. Every modern application uses them; every concurrent bug starts with them.

Core concepts

1. Threads vs processes. A process has one or more threads. Each thread has its own program counter, registers, and stack — but threads in one process share the heap, code, and open files. Creating a thread is much cheaper than forking a process. Crashes in one thread typically kill the whole process.

2. User-level vs kernel-level threads. Kernel-level: the OS schedules each thread directly. Native threads on Linux/Windows. Performance scales with CPU cores. User-level: a runtime library schedules threads inside one kernel process; older Java, modern Go goroutines (via M:N mapping). Each model trades capability for overhead.

3. Why multithread. Parallelism — using multiple CPU cores. Concurrency — overlapping I/O while computing. Responsiveness — one thread for the UI, others for slow work. Modular structure — naturally separate concerns into separate threads. Different motivations, often combined.

4. The M:N threading model. Many user-level threads multiplexed onto fewer kernel threads. Go does this with goroutines on top of an OS thread pool. Lets you spawn millions of lightweight threads without exhausting kernel resources. Java added virtual threads (Project Loom) for the same reason.

5. Thread creation primitives. POSIX: pthread_create, pthread_join. Java: Thread, ExecutorService, virtual threads. C#: Task, Thread. Each platform exposes the OS primitives plus higher-level abstractions. Application code increasingly uses pools and tasks rather than raw thread creation.

6. Thread-local storage. Variables that are global per-thread but separate across threads. Useful for context (current user, request ID) without passing parameters everywhere. Costs: memory per thread, careful cleanup on thread exit. Heavy use is sometimes a sign of design problems.

7. The cost of threads. Each thread typically reserves 1-8 MB of stack space. A thread per HTTP request limits servers to thousands; a goroutine per request scales to millions. Production servers use thread pools, async I/O, or virtual threads to keep thread counts bounded.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Spawning unbounded threads — eventually OOM or scheduler thrash.
  • Sharing mutable state without synchronization — race conditions, hard-to-reproduce bugs.
  • Treating threads as cheap — they are cheaper than processes, not free.
  • Confusing concurrency (interleaving) with parallelism (simultaneous execution) — single-core CPUs can be concurrent without being parallel.

Quick recap

Threads share memory within one process; processes do not. Kernel-level threads scale across cores; user-level threads can be millions but require runtime support (M:N). Threads bring parallelism, concurrency, responsiveness, and modular structure — at the cost of synchronization complexity and stack memory. Thread pools and virtual threads bound the cost.

Glossary

Thread
An independent execution path within a process, sharing memory with other threads.
Kernel-level thread
Thread scheduled directly by the OS.
User-level thread
Thread scheduled by a userspace runtime; cheaper, less hardware-aware.
M:N threading
Many user-level threads multiplexed onto fewer kernel threads.
Thread pool
Reusable set of worker threads that execute submitted tasks.

📊 FIGURE — how this section fits together

📖 Worked example — pipes vs shared memory

WORKED EXAMPLE — two processes must exchange data
Message passing (pipe): cat log.txt | grep error — the shell wires cat’s stdout to grep’s stdin through a kernel buffer. Every byte crosses the kernel (two copies), but synchronization is FREE: grep blocks until data arrives, cat blocks when the pipe fills.

Shared memory: both processes map the same region; after setup, reads/writes are plain memory access — the FASTEST IPC, zero kernel involvement per access. But now the processes must synchronize themselves (semaphores/mutexes) or race.

Trade: pipes/messages = simpler + safer + slower; shared memory = fastest + you own the locking. Sockets extend message passing across machines.
⚠️ WHO SYNCHRONIZES?
Message passing: the kernel does (blocking send/receive). Shared memory: YOU do. That one-line contrast answers most IPC comparison questions.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Processes have separate address spaces — they cannot share memory directly. IPC is how they communicate anyway. Every multi-process system, every microservices architecture, every command pipeline is built on IPC mechanisms. Knowing the options and their tradeoffs is essential for building anything beyond a single-process program.

Core concepts

1. Pipes — the original Unix IPC. A unidirectional byte stream between two processes. Anonymous pipes connect parent and child (the | shell operator). Named pipes (FIFOs) live in the file system and can connect unrelated processes. Cheap, simple, byte-stream — ideal for command-line tools, awkward for structured data.

2. Message queues. POSIX message queues (mq_open, mq_send) and SysV (msgget) deliver discrete messages between processes. Each message has a type and a payload. Higher-level than pipes; more setup. Distributed message queues (RabbitMQ, Kafka) extend this idea across the network.

3. Shared memory. Two processes map the same physical memory pages into their address spaces. Fastest IPC available — no copying. But sharing memory across address spaces requires explicit synchronization (semaphores, mutexes). POSIX shm_open, SysV shmget. Used by databases, browsers, high-performance servers.

4. Sockets — IPC and network in one API. Unix domain sockets (AF_UNIX) for local IPC, network sockets (AF_INET) for remote. Same API. Bidirectional, byte-stream or datagram. The most general IPC — extends naturally to network protocols. Modern microservices use sockets for nearly all communication.

5. Signals. Asynchronous notifications: SIGTERM (please exit), SIGKILL (forced exit), SIGINT (Ctrl-C), SIGHUP, SIGUSR1/2. Cannot carry data beyond the signal number. Restricted: only async-signal-safe functions can run inside handlers. Useful for control, dangerous for general communication.

6. Memory-mapped files. mmap a file into multiple processes' address spaces; reads and writes go through page cache. Combines persistence with shared memory. Used for caches, large datasets, IPC where one writer and many readers share a data file.

7. Choosing an IPC mechanism. Local-only structured data, low-volume — pipes or message queues. Local high-volume — shared memory or Unix sockets. Local OR remote — sockets. Async notification — signals. Persistent shared state — memory-mapped files. Fit choice to scale, persistence, and locality.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Using shared memory without synchronization — data races, corrupted structures.
  • Trying to carry data via signals beyond the signal number — undefined behavior; use a different mechanism.
  • Defaulting to TCP loopback when Unix sockets would be 2-3x faster for local-only IPC.
  • Leaking pipes, FIFOs, or shared memory segments — they can persist after process death and accumulate.

Quick recap

Pipes for unidirectional byte streams. Message queues for discrete typed messages. Shared memory for fastest local communication (with explicit synchronization). Sockets for everything that might cross the network. Signals for async control notifications. Memory-mapped files for persistent shared state. Match mechanism to scale, persistence, and whether the boundary is local or networked.

Glossary

IPC
Inter-Process Communication — mechanisms for processes to exchange data.
Pipe
Unidirectional byte stream; anonymous (related processes) or named FIFO.
Shared memory
Memory pages mapped into multiple processes' address spaces.
Unix domain socket
Socket using local file system path; same API as network sockets.
Signal
Asynchronous OS-delivered notification carrying only a signal number.

📘 Deep dive: TCP vs UDP & channel direction

TCP is connection-oriented and reliable: handshake first, ordered delivery, retransmission of lost packets — use for web pages, email, file transfer. UDP is connectionless and unreliable-by-design: no handshake, no retransmission, minimal overhead — use for streaming, gaming, DNS, where speed beats perfection. Channel direction: simplex is one-way only (broadcast), half-duplex alternates (walkie-talkie), full-duplex flows both ways at once (phone call).

Synchronous communication blocks the caller until the response arrives (a phone call, a blocking API request). Asynchronous lets the caller continue and be notified later (email, message queues) — the tradeoff is simplicity vs responsiveness.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — a race condition, instruction by instruction

WORKED EXAMPLE — two threads, balance = balance + 100
balance = 500. Each thread runs: LOAD balance → ADD 100 → STORE.
T1: LOAD 500
T2: LOAD 500        ← interleaved before T1 stores!
T1: ADD → 600, STORE 600
T2: ADD → 600, STORE 600   ← final: 600, not 700. $100 vanished.
The three-instruction read-modify-write is not atomic; the outcome depends on interleaving — the definition of a race. The fix: make the update a critical section only one thread may enter at a time, satisfying mutual exclusion + progress + bounded waiting.
⚠️ RACES HIDE IN “ONE LINE” OF CODE
balance += 100 LOOKS atomic in C/Java — it compiles to 3+ instructions. “Which code has a race?” → any unsynchronized shared read-modify-write, no matter how short it looks.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

When threads or processes share data without coordination, the timing of their interleaving determines the result. Sometimes correct, sometimes corrupt. A race condition is the most common, hardest-to-reproduce bug in concurrent systems. Recognizing critical sections — the regions that need protection — is the first step to writing safe concurrent code.

Core concepts

1. What a race condition is. Two or more threads access shared state, at least one writes, with no synchronization. The outcome depends on the order in which the OS interleaves their instructions. Sometimes you see the bug; usually you don't, until production load makes it frequent.

2. Atomicity at the hardware level. What looks like a single statement may not be atomic. counter++ compiles to load, increment, store. Two threads can both load the same value, increment, and store — losing one increment. Single-instruction increments exist (x86's lock add) but compilers don't always emit them.

3. Critical sections. A region of code that accesses shared state and must execute as a unit. Marking critical sections explicitly — with locks, semaphores, atomics — is how you turn 'might race' into 'guaranteed serialized.'

4. Three properties of a correct solution. Mutual exclusion (only one thread in the critical section at a time). Progress (if no thread is in it, a waiting thread eventually enters). Bounded waiting (a waiting thread eventually enters; no starvation). Any synchronization scheme must satisfy all three.

5. Why naive solutions fail. Disabling interrupts works on single-CPU but not on multicore. Strict alternation deadlocks if one thread doesn't try to enter. Test-and-set busy-waits but is correct. Peterson's algorithm works in software but is complex. Real systems use hardware atomic instructions plus higher-level primitives.

6. Memory consistency wrinkles. Modern CPUs reorder instructions and have per-core caches. Without memory barriers, even correctly-locked code can see stale values from another core. Most synchronization primitives include implicit barriers; raw atomic operations may not. Java's volatile, C's atomic with memory_order, and Rust's Ordering all expose this.

7. Why this gets harder, not easier. More cores, more threads, more shared state. Languages add atomics and lock-free data structures, but the underlying hazards grow with parallelism. The discipline of identifying critical sections explicitly is more important now than at any point in computing's past.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Believing a one-line statement is atomic — usually it isn't.
  • Adding 'volatile' (in C/C++) and assuming it provides synchronization — it doesn't.
  • Locking individual operations but failing to lock multi-step invariants — you protect the steps but not the relationship.
  • Reproducing a race condition as 'works on my machine' and shipping it — production load will find it.

Quick recap

A race condition is unsynchronized concurrent access to shared state with at least one writer. A critical section is the protected region. Correct solutions provide mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting. Hardware atomics and memory barriers are the underlying primitives; language-level locks and atomics build on them. Be explicit about critical sections; assume nothing about atomicity.

Glossary

Race condition
Bug where program behavior depends on unpredictable thread interleaving.
Critical section
Code region accessing shared state that must execute as a unit.
Mutual exclusion
Property that only one thread is in the critical section at a time.
Atomic operation
Operation guaranteed indivisible by hardware or runtime.
Memory barrier
Instruction enforcing ordering of memory operations across cores.

📖 Worked example — mutex and semaphore, used correctly

WORKED EXAMPLE — fix the race + limit a pool
// MUTEX — exactly one thread in the critical section
acquire(lock);
balance = balance + 100;
release(lock);

// COUNTING SEMAPHORE — at most 3 users of a connection pool
sem = semaphore(3);
wait(sem);      // 4th caller BLOCKS here until someone signals
useConnection();
signal(sem);
Mutex = binary ownership (lock/unlock by the same thread). Counting semaphore = N permits — wait decrements (blocking at 0), signal increments. Under the hood both need an ATOMIC hardware primitive (test-and-set / compare-and-swap) — you cannot build safe locks from ordinary loads and stores.
⚠️ SPINLOCK vs BLOCKING
A spinlock busy-waits (burns CPU — fine for tiny waits on multicore); a blocking mutex sleeps the thread (context switch — right for longer waits). “Which wastes CPU while waiting?” → the spinlock.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Once you've identified critical sections, you need primitives that enforce safe access. Mutexes, semaphores, condition variables, monitors — each addresses a different coordination need. Picking the right one and using it correctly is the working skill of concurrent programming.

Core concepts

1. Mutex (mutual exclusion lock). The simplest primitive: at most one thread holds the lock at a time. lock() blocks until acquired; unlock() releases. Fundamental for protecting critical sections. Always lock and unlock in matching pairs — try/finally in most languages.

2. Semaphore — counting permits. Holds an integer count. wait (or P) decrements; if zero, blocks. signal (or V) increments and wakes a waiter. Counting semaphores limit concurrent access (e.g., max 5 connections). Binary semaphores are like mutexes (but without ownership tracking).

3. Condition variables. Allow a thread to wait for a specific condition to become true. wait() atomically releases an associated lock and sleeps; signal() wakes one waiter, broadcast() wakes all. Always wait inside a while loop checking the condition — spurious wakeups happen.

4. Monitors and synchronized methods. A monitor combines a mutex with condition variables, scoped to a class or object. Java's synchronized methods, C#'s lock, classic Hoare/Mesa monitors. Higher-level than raw mutexes; harder to misuse.

5. Read-write locks. Multiple readers can hold simultaneously; writers are exclusive. Useful when reads vastly outnumber writes. More complex bookkeeping; not always faster than a plain mutex — measure before assuming.

6. Barriers and latches. A barrier blocks N threads until all N have arrived, then releases all at once. Useful for parallel algorithms with phases. Latches (Java's CountDownLatch) count down — release when count reaches zero.

7. Spin locks. Busy-wait instead of sleeping. Cheap when contention is rare and critical sections are very short. Wasteful otherwise. Used in kernel and some lock-free libraries; rarely the right tool in application code.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Forgetting to release a lock on the error path — deadlock. Use RAII, try/finally, or with statements.
  • Using condition variable signals without holding the associated lock — race against waiters.
  • Deciding between mutex and read-write lock without measuring — readers don't always benefit at high concurrency.
  • Spin locking in user space for long-held locks — wastes CPU and starves other threads.

Quick recap

Mutexes for exclusive access. Semaphores for counted permits. Condition variables for waiting on predicates. Monitors bundle mutex plus condition vars. Read-write locks for read-heavy workloads. Barriers and latches for phased parallelism. Spin locks for very short critical sections. Match primitive to coordination need.

Glossary

Mutex
Lock allowing at most one holder; the basic mutual-exclusion primitive.
Semaphore
Counter-based primitive: wait decrements, signal increments.
Condition variable
Lets threads sleep until a predicate becomes true; pairs with a mutex.
Monitor
Object encapsulating mutex and condition variables for safe shared-state methods.
Read-write lock
Multiple-reader, single-writer lock for read-heavy workloads.

📖 Worked example — producer-consumer, solved with semaphores

WORKED EXAMPLE — bounded buffer of size 5
empty = semaphore(5)   # free slots
full  = semaphore(0)   # filled slots
mutex = semaphore(1)   # buffer protection

Producer:                    Consumer:
wait(empty)                  wait(full)
wait(mutex)                  wait(mutex)
  add item                     remove item
signal(mutex)                signal(mutex)
signal(full)                 signal(empty)
empty stops producers when the buffer is full; full stops consumers when it’s empty; mutex guards the actual insertion. The ORDER matters: wait(mutex) BEFORE wait(empty) can deadlock (holding the lock while blocked). This one pattern also decodes readers-writers and dining philosophers — same primitives, different constraints.
⚠️ THE SWAPPED-WAITS TRAP
The classic exam bug: producer takes mutex, then waits on empty while holding it — consumer can never get the mutex to signal empty. Deadlock by lock-ordering; always acquire the counting semaphore first.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

A handful of named problems — producer-consumer, readers-writers, dining philosophers — pop up in countless real systems disguised as something else. Studying them gives you a vocabulary for recognizing patterns in your own code and applying proven solutions instead of reinventing.

Core concepts

1. Producer-Consumer (Bounded Buffer). One or more producers add items to a buffer; one or more consumers remove them. Buffer has capacity. Coordination needs: producers wait when full, consumers wait when empty, mutual exclusion on the buffer itself. Solved with a mutex plus two condition variables, or a counting semaphore. Foundation of every BlockingQueue.

2. Readers-Writers. Many threads want to read; some want to write. Concurrent reads are fine; writes are exclusive. Several variants: readers-preference (writers may starve), writers-preference (readers may starve), fair (alternating). Read-write locks implement this; choose policy based on workload.

3. Dining Philosophers. Five philosophers sit at a round table with five forks between them. Each needs both adjacent forks to eat. Naive 'pick up left, then right' deadlocks if all pick up left simultaneously. Solutions: enforce ordering (number forks, pick lower-numbered first), allow at most four to attempt, or use a waiter that grants permission. Models any resource-allocation problem.

4. Sleeping Barber. A barber shop has one barber, N waiting chairs. Customers leave if no chair is free. Coordination: barber sleeps when shop empty, customer wakes barber, barber takes one customer at a time. Models call-center / request-handler designs.

5. Cigarette Smokers. An agent has three ingredients; three smokers each have one of three. Each smoker needs both other ingredients. Models complex multi-resource matching where producers can't be modified — the constraint is the educational point.

6. Recognizing the patterns in real code. A web server with a connection pool? Producer-consumer + readers-writers. A database with row locking? Dining philosophers (lock ordering avoids deadlock). A thread pool? Bounded buffer of tasks. Naming the pattern lets you reason about it with proven techniques.

7. Why correctness is harder than it looks. Even named problems with textbook solutions have subtle bugs in real implementations: missed signals, lost wakeups, priority inversion. Concurrent code reviews should be specific: 'what happens if this thread is preempted right here?' rather than 'looks fine.'

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Solving Dining Philosophers with naive 'left then right' — guaranteed deadlock under load.
  • Implementing producer-consumer with one condition variable — wakes the wrong thread types, loses signals.
  • Assuming readers-writers preference doesn't matter — under heavy load, the 'losing' side starves.
  • Reinventing a classical solution in a real system — usually slower, buggier, and harder to review than using a well-tested implementation.

Quick recap

Producer-Consumer: bounded buffers with full/empty signaling. Readers-Writers: many readers OR one writer, with starvation policy. Dining Philosophers: resource ordering or arbiters prevent deadlock. Sleeping Barber, Cigarette Smokers, and others model variations. The patterns recur in real systems; recognizing them enables proven solutions.

Glossary

Producer-Consumer
Pattern: producers add to a bounded buffer; consumers remove; both must wait when buffer is full / empty.
Readers-Writers
Pattern: concurrent reads allowed, writes exclusive.
Dining Philosophers
Classical problem modeling deadlock-prone resource allocation.
Bounded buffer
Fixed-capacity queue between producers and consumers.
Lock ordering
Acquire locks in a consistent order to prevent circular wait deadlock.

Why concurrency at all: throughput (more work per second), responsiveness (UI stays alive while work runs), and parallelism (many cores actually used). Synchronization overhead: locks slow programs — contention, context switches, and serialized critical sections eat the gains if locking is coarse. Lock-free algorithms sidestep locks entirely using atomic operations (compare-and-swap): no thread ever blocks holding a lock, at the price of trickier reasoning.

📖 Worked example — deadlock detected with a Banker’s-style check

WORKED EXAMPLE — is this state safe?
10 total instances. P1 holds 4, may need 4 more; P2 holds 3, may need 2 more; free = 3.
• Can P2 finish with 3 free? needs 2 ≤ 3 ✓ → run P2, reclaim its 3 → free = 6.
• Can P1 finish? needs 4 ≤ 6 ✓ → free = 10.
A completion order exists → the state is SAFE. If P2 had needed 4, neither could finish with free = 3 → unsafe (deadlock risk).

The four required conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait) all had to hold for danger to exist; avoidance (Banker’s) refuses allocations leading to unsafe states, prevention breaks one condition outright (e.g., acquire all resources up front, or order resources globally).
⚠️ UNSAFE ≠ DEADLOCKED
Unsafe means a deadlock is POSSIBLE, not certain. Deadlocked means the cycle exists NOW (detectable in the resource-allocation graph). Exams test that distinction verbatim.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Deadlock is when two or more threads or processes wait on each other forever. Production deadlocks freeze the system without any warning except 'why did everything stop?' Understanding the conditions that cause deadlock — and the strategies to prevent, avoid, detect, or recover from it — is essential for any concurrent system.

Core concepts

1. The four Coffman conditions — all required. Mutual exclusion: a resource can only be held by one thread. Hold and wait: threads hold resources while requesting more. No preemption: resources can't be forcibly taken away. Circular wait: a cycle of threads each waiting for the next. Removing any one breaks deadlock.

2. Prevention strategies. Eliminate hold-and-wait by acquiring all resources atomically. Eliminate circular wait by enforcing a global lock order. Eliminate no-preemption by allowing rollback. Eliminate mutual exclusion (rare; some resources are inherently exclusive). Each strategy has costs.

3. Lock ordering — the practical favorite. Define a global ordering on all locks. Always acquire in the same order. No cycle ⇒ no deadlock. Simple, effective, easy to review. Costs: must know the ordering everywhere, and library locks complicate the picture.

4. Avoidance — the Banker's Algorithm. Allocate resources only when the system stays in a 'safe state' — one where some sequence of completions is possible. Requires advance knowledge of maximum needs. Theoretical interest > practical use; production systems rarely have the prerequisite information.

5. Detection and recovery. Allow deadlocks to occur; detect via wait-for graph cycles; recover by aborting one or more processes. Database systems use this pattern — detect deadlock, abort the youngest transaction, retry. Acceptable when retries are cheap and deadlocks are rare.

6. Livelock and starvation. Livelock: threads change state in response to each other but make no progress (two people stepping aside in a hallway). Starvation: a thread never gets a resource because others keep taking it. Both look like deadlock but require different fixes (backoff, fair scheduling).

7. Real-world deadlock signs. Process or thread CPU drops to zero. Locks held but no progress. Database queries time out across the board. Tools: jstack (Java thread dumps), gdb attach (native), lsof, /proc/PID/wchan. Most modern monitors flag deadlocks automatically.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Acquiring locks in different orders in different code paths — deadlock waiting to happen.
  • Holding a lock while calling unknown code (callbacks, listeners) — they may try to acquire other locks.
  • Mistaking livelock or starvation for deadlock — different symptoms, different fixes.
  • Ignoring deadlocks in design and 'handling them in production' — most production deadlocks are designed in, not random.

Quick recap

Deadlock requires all four Coffman conditions; remove any one to prevent. Lock ordering is the most practical strategy. Avoidance via Banker's Algorithm rarely fits real systems. Detect-and-recover is common in databases. Livelock and starvation are related but distinct. Production diagnosis uses thread dumps and lock-waiting graphs.

Glossary

Deadlock
State where two or more threads wait on each other forever.
Coffman conditions
Four conditions required for deadlock: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait.
Lock ordering
Prevention strategy: always acquire locks in a fixed global order.
Banker's Algorithm
Avoidance strategy granting requests only if the system stays in a safe state.
Livelock
State where threads keep changing state but make no progress.
📊 FIGURE — the four ways to handle deadlock
🎯 EXAM TIP
The ostrich algorithm means ignoring deadlock — the name is the joke about burying your head in the sand. It is the pragmatic choice most general-purpose operating systems make, Linux included, because deadlocks are rare enough that the performance and complexity cost of prevention or avoidance is not repaid.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — first-fit vs best-fit, computed

WORKED EXAMPLE — place a 25 KB job in holes [30, 60, 20, 40]
• First-fit: scan from the start, take the first hole that fits → the 30 KB hole (leaves 5).
• Best-fit: smallest hole that fits → the 30 KB hole here too — but with holes [60, 28, 40]: best-fit picks 28 (leaves 3), first-fit picks 60 (leaves 35).
• Worst-fit: biggest hole (60), betting big leftovers stay usable.

All three suffer external fragmentation: after churn, free memory splinters into holes too small to use even though the TOTAL is plenty. Compaction (sliding everything together) fixes it at high cost — paging (next section) sidesteps it entirely.
⚠️ EXTERNAL vs INTERNAL FRAGMENTATION
External = wasted space BETWEEN allocations (variable partitions). Internal = wasted space INSIDE an allocation (fixed blocks/pages rounded up). Paging eliminates external but keeps a little internal (half a page per process on average).
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Before virtual memory, the OS had to fit programs into physical RAM directly. The strategies developed then — fixed partitions, dynamic partitions, fragmentation handling — still inform modern allocators (heap, slab, buddy). Understanding them is the foundation for understanding paging, virtual memory, and why your malloc behaves the way it does.

Core concepts

1. Fixed partitioning. Divide memory into a fixed number of regions at boot. Each process loaded into one. Simple but wasteful — internal fragmentation when a process is smaller than its region. Used in early multiprogramming systems; almost extinct today.

2. Dynamic partitioning. Allocate exactly what each process needs. As processes load and exit, free space fragments. External fragmentation: total free space is enough but no contiguous chunk fits. Workarounds: compaction (expensive), or paging (next section).

3. First-fit, best-fit, worst-fit. First-fit: scan free list, take first big-enough block. Fast. Best-fit: smallest block ≥ request. Less waste, more search. Worst-fit: largest block. Counter-intuitively sometimes leaves usable remainders. First-fit is the practical winner; best-fit is theoretically attractive but worse in practice.

4. Internal vs external fragmentation. Internal: allocated block is bigger than the request — waste inside the block. Common in fixed-size allocators. External: enough total free space, but no contiguous block fits the request. Common in dynamic allocators. Different problems, different fixes.

5. Buddy allocator. Splits memory into power-of-two blocks. Each request rounds up to a power of two. Free blocks merge with their 'buddy' when both are free. Used in Linux's kernel page allocator. Fast; some internal fragmentation.

6. Slab allocator. For frequent same-size allocations (kernel objects, networking buffers). Pre-carved into fixed-size slots; allocation and free are O(1). Linux's kernel uses slab caches per object type. Avoids fragmentation by design.

7. Modern userspace allocators. ptmalloc (glibc), tcmalloc (Google), jemalloc (Facebook), mimalloc (Microsoft). Per-thread arenas, size classes, large-block strategies. Performance differences of 2-10x on contended workloads. Production systems often pick a specific allocator deliberately.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Choosing best-fit because it 'sounds smart' — first-fit usually wins in practice.
  • Ignoring fragmentation — long-running processes' heaps grow even when 'memory' isn't needed.
  • Mixing allocator behaviors (kernel page allocator vs userspace malloc) — they solve different problems at different layers.
  • Defaulting to glibc malloc on heavily-threaded servers without measuring — switching to jemalloc or tcmalloc often gives free wins.

Quick recap

Fixed and dynamic partitioning are the foundational strategies. First-fit is the practical default. Buddy allocators trade some internal fragmentation for speed and merging. Slab allocators handle fixed-size kernel objects. Modern userspace allocators use per-thread arenas and size classes. Choose based on workload, not aesthetics.

Glossary

Fixed partitioning
Memory divided into static regions at boot.
Dynamic partitioning
Memory regions sized to fit each process; suffers external fragmentation.
Internal fragmentation
Wasted space inside an allocated block.
External fragmentation
Free space scattered across non-contiguous gaps.
Buddy / slab allocator
Specialized allocators using power-of-two splits or fixed-size slots.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — translate an address through a page table

WORKED EXAMPLE — 4 KB pages, by the numbers
Virtual address 8300, page size 4096:
• Page number = 8300 ÷ 4096 = 2; offset = 8300 − 8192 = 108.
• Page table entry [2] says frame 7.
• Physical address = 7 × 4096 + 108 = 28,780.
Pages are fixed-size, so ANY free frame serves ANY page — no external fragmentation, and the process’s memory needn’t be contiguous. The TLB caches recent translations so this lookup usually costs nothing.
⚠️ PAGE = VIRTUAL, FRAME = PHYSICAL
Pages live in the process’s virtual space; frames are the physical slots they land in. Same size, different worlds — swap the words in an answer and it’s wrong. Multi-level tables exist because a flat table for a 64-bit space would be absurdly large.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Paging is one of the most influential ideas in computing. By splitting memory into fixed-size pages and decoupling virtual addresses from physical, the OS gives every process its own private address space, enables swapping, and isolates programs from each other. Every modern OS pages; understanding it is non-negotiable for OS literacy.

Core concepts

1. Virtual vs physical addresses. A program sees virtual addresses; the CPU's MMU translates each to a physical address before hitting RAM. Each process has its own virtual address space; the kernel maintains a page table mapping its virtual pages to physical frames.

2. Pages and frames. Page: a fixed-size chunk of virtual memory (typically 4 KB on x86). Frame: a fixed-size chunk of physical memory. The page table maps page numbers to frame numbers. Pages of one process can be in any frame, in any order, or absent (paged out).

3. Page table structure. A virtual address splits into page number + offset. Page number indexes the page table; the entry yields the frame number; offset stays the same. With 32-bit addresses and 4 KB pages, 1 million entries per process — too big for one flat table. Hence multi-level page tables.

4. Multi-level page tables. Two, three, or four levels of indirection. Top-level entries point to mid-level tables that point to leaves. Most processes only fill in a few entries; multi-level avoids allocating an entire table for sparse address spaces. x86-64 uses four levels.

5. The TLB — Translation Lookaside Buffer. Page table walks are slow (multiple memory accesses per translation). The MMU caches recent translations in the TLB — typically 64 to 1024 entries. TLB hits are nearly free; misses trigger a page-table walk. TLB efficiency dominates large-memory workloads.

6. Permissions and protection bits. Each page-table entry includes flags: present (in physical memory), readable, writable, executable, user-accessible, dirty (modified), accessed. The OS enforces read-only data, no-execute stacks, kernel/user separation through these bits.

7. Why paging enables so much. Per-process address spaces (isolation). Demand paging (load only what's used). Swapping (extend memory beyond physical RAM). Shared memory (map same frame into multiple processes). Memory-mapped files (frames backed by file blocks). Copy-on-write fork (shared frames marked read-only until write).

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Confusing virtual address layout (process-visible) with physical layout (kernel-visible).
  • Underestimating the TLB — heavy random-access workloads spend more time on translation than computation.
  • Treating page size as fixed at 4 KB — modern CPUs support huge pages (2 MB, 1 GB) for large-memory apps.
  • Assuming permissions are checked once — the MMU re-checks on every access; a wrong setting breaks at runtime, not load time.

Quick recap

Paging splits memory into fixed pages and decouples virtual from physical addresses. Page tables map virtual pages to physical frames; multi-level structures keep them compact. The TLB caches translations to make this fast. Permissions live per page. Paging is what enables process isolation, virtual memory, sharing, and copy-on-write.

Glossary

Page
Fixed-size chunk of virtual memory (typically 4 KB).
Frame
Fixed-size chunk of physical memory.
Page table
Per-process structure mapping virtual pages to physical frames.
TLB
Translation Lookaside Buffer — MMU cache of recent virtual-to-physical translations.
Multi-level page table
Tree of tables avoiding allocation of full address-space mapping.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — FIFO vs LRU on the same reference string

WORKED EXAMPLE — 1,2,3,4,1,2,5 with 3 frames
FIFO: 1F 2F 3F | 4 evicts 1 → F | 1 evicts 2 → F | 2 evicts 3 → F | 5 evicts 4 → F = 7 faults.
LRU: 1F 2F 3F | 4 evicts 1 (least recent) F | 1 evicts 2 F | 2 evicts 3 F | 5 evicts 4 F = 7 here too — but on strings with re-use locality LRU wins consistently, and OPT (evict the page used furthest in future) is the unreachable ideal used as a yardstick.

When faults dominate runtime — pages constantly evicted then immediately needed — that’s thrashing: too many processes squeezed into too little RAM. The cure is fewer processes (working-set admission), not a faster disk.
⚠️ BELADY’S ANOMALY
With FIFO, MORE frames can produce MORE faults on some strings — famously counterintuitive and famously tested. LRU never suffers it (it’s a stack algorithm).
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

With paging in place, the OS can pretend each process has more memory than physically exists. Pages live on disk when not in use and are loaded on demand. Choosing which pages to evict — page replacement — is one of the most studied problems in OS research, because every choice affects performance dramatically.

Core concepts

1. Demand paging. Pages aren't loaded until first accessed. The page-table entry is marked 'not present'; the access triggers a page fault. The OS allocates a frame, loads from disk, updates the entry, and resumes the instruction. Saves memory and startup time at the cost of fault overhead.

2. The page fault handler. On fault, the kernel decides: legitimate access to a swapped or yet-to-load page (handle and resume), or invalid access (segfault). The path through the kernel is one of the hottest in the system; OS designers tune it heavily.

3. Page replacement — the core problem. When a fault occurs and no free frames exist, evict an existing page. The choice affects every subsequent access. Algorithms target one goal: minimize future page faults, given limited information.

4. FIFO (First-In, First-Out). Evict the oldest-loaded page. Simple, but suffers Belady's anomaly — adding more frames can increase faults. Educational, not used in production.

5. Optimal (Belady's algorithm). Evict the page used furthest in the future. Provably minimum faults. Requires knowing the future — impossible in practice. Used as a benchmark to compare other algorithms against.

6. LRU (Least Recently Used). Evict the page unused longest. Approximates Optimal under temporal locality. Costly in pure form (timestamp every access); approximated in practice with reference bits and clock algorithms.

7. Clock algorithm — practical LRU approximation. Frames in a circular list. A 'reference bit' is set on access. When choosing victim, scan: if bit is 1, clear it and continue; if 0, evict. Cheap to implement, close to LRU in behavior, used in real kernels including Linux.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Implementing pure LRU — timestamping every memory access is too expensive at scale.
  • FIFO in production — Belady's anomaly is real; more memory can mean more faults.
  • Ignoring locality — random workloads are pessimal for any reference-based algorithm.
  • Confusing 'page replacement policy' with 'allocation policy' — the first chooses victims, the second chooses how many frames each process gets.

Quick recap

Demand paging loads pages on first access, triggering page faults. The handler manages frame allocation and eviction. FIFO is simple but flawed (Belady's anomaly). Optimal is the theoretical bound. LRU approximates Optimal under locality. Clock algorithm makes LRU cheap and is what real kernels actually use.

Glossary

Demand paging
Loading pages from disk only when first accessed.
Page fault
Trap raised when a process accesses a page not currently in physical memory.
Page replacement
Choosing which page to evict to make room for a new one.
LRU
Least Recently Used — replacement policy evicting longest-unused page.
Clock algorithm
Cheap LRU approximation using a reference bit and circular scan.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

If processes collectively need more pages than physical memory holds, the system spends more time paging than computing. This is thrashing — and it's catastrophic. The working-set model and related ideas exist specifically to detect, prevent, and recover from this failure mode.

Core concepts

1. What thrashing looks like. CPU utilization plummets, disk I/O spikes, response times collapse. Processes fault on pages, evict another process's pages, that process faults — endless replacement with no useful work. A user-visible 'system feels stuck' even though CPUs are technically active.

2. The cause: insufficient frames per process. If each process has too few resident frames to hold its currently-needed pages, every memory access nearly faults. The system is the most memory-starved when running the most processes — the opposite of intent.

3. The working set. The set of pages a process has accessed in the last τ time units. If the working set fits in physical memory, faults are rare. If not, thrashing. The working set changes over time as program phases change (initialization → steady state → cleanup).

4. Working set strategy. Track each process's working set; only schedule it to run if its working set fits. If total working sets exceed memory, suspend some processes (move out of ready queue) until the rest can run without thrashing. Crude but effective.

5. Page fault frequency (PFF) heuristic. Watch each process's fault rate. Above a high threshold: give it more frames. Below a low threshold: take frames away. Reactive, simpler than tracking working sets explicitly.

6. Modern systems and swapping. On servers with abundant RAM, thrashing is rare. On laptops and phones, swap is small and aggressive memory pressure triggers OOM kill rather than degraded paging. Cloud workloads tune memory limits explicitly to avoid both swap and OOM.

7. The lesson for application engineers. Memory pressure surfaces as terrible latency long before processes get killed. Monitoring should track page fault rate, swap activity, and resident set size. A box that looks 'fine' on CPU graphs can be unusably slow because of paging. Always keep memory headroom.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Overcommitting memory to maximize utilization — the slope from 'tight' to 'thrashing' is sudden.
  • Assuming swap is 'extra memory' — it is several orders of magnitude slower than RAM.
  • Ignoring page fault rate as a metric — it's the most direct signal of memory pressure.
  • Tuning processes individually without considering aggregate working set — interaction effects are real.

Quick recap

Thrashing happens when collective working sets exceed physical memory; the system pages itself to a halt. The working-set model tracks pages used recently and admits only processes whose working sets fit. PFF is a simpler reactive heuristic. Modern cloud systems avoid swap and use memory limits + OOM kill instead. Page fault rate is the signal to watch.

Glossary

Thrashing
Pathological state where the system spends most of its time paging instead of computing.
Working set
Set of pages a process has accessed in a recent time window.
Resident set
Pages of a process actually present in physical memory at a given moment.
Page fault frequency (PFF)
Rate of faults; used as a heuristic for memory pressure.
Swap
Disk-backed extension of virtual memory; orders of magnitude slower than RAM.

📖 Worked example — what happens on open()/read()

WORKED EXAMPLE — resolving /home/nat/notes.txt
1. The path resolves component by component: the root directory locates home, home’s directory entry locates nat, nat’s locates notes.txt → its inode (the metadata record: owner, permissions, size, timestamps, block pointers).
2. Permission check against your user/group.
3. A file descriptor (say fd 3) is handed back — an index into your process’s open-file table, carrying the current offset.
4. read(3, buf, 100) follows the inode’s block pointers, advances the offset by 100.
A directory is just a special file mapping names → inode numbers. Hard links = two names, one inode (link count 2); symlinks = a file containing a path.
⚠️ THE NAME IS NOT THE FILE
The inode IS the file; names merely point at it. Deleting one hard link only decrements the count — data dies when the LAST link (and last open fd) goes. Standard exam trap.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Files are the longest-lived, most user-visible OS abstraction. Every program reads or writes them. Every backup, every deployment, every security policy is built on file semantics — names, permissions, types, timestamps. Understanding what a file is and how directories organize them is foundational.

Core concepts

1. What a file is, OS-side. A named, persistent collection of bytes. The OS associates metadata with each file: size, type, owner, permissions, timestamps, location on disk. Programs see the bytes; the OS bookkeeping happens behind the scenes.

2. File operations. create, open, read, write, seek, close, delete, rename, truncate. Each maps to a system call. open returns a file descriptor (Unix) or handle (Windows) that subsequent operations use. Most file APIs are some skin over these primitives.

3. File types. Regular files (data). Directories (special files mapping names to file IDs). Symbolic links (pointer to another path). Hard links (additional name for the same file). Device files (interface to hardware on Unix). Named pipes / sockets (IPC). The same OS file API handles them all.

4. Paths — absolute and relative. Absolute: starts from the root (/, C:\). Relative: starts from the current working directory. The kernel resolves paths through directory traversal, checking permissions at each level. '..' moves up; '.' stays put.

5. Permissions and ownership (Unix model). Three permission bits — read, write, execute — for three classes — owner, group, other. ls -l shows them as rwxr-xr--. ACLs extend this with finer control. Windows uses a richer ACL-based model. Unix's nine-bit model is simple and ubiquitous.

6. Hard links vs symbolic links. Hard link: another name for the same inode (same file). Both names equally valid; file is gone when last name is removed. Symbolic link: a pathname pointing to another path. Following requires reading the link. Different semantics; different uses.

7. File metadata and stat. stat() returns size, owner, mode, link count, timestamps (atime, mtime, ctime), device and inode numbers. Foundational for ls, find, backup tools, version control. Performance tools (ls of huge directories) optimize for batch stat operations.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Confusing hard links and symbolic links — they have different lifecycle and ownership semantics.
  • Assuming Unix permissions cover all access control needs — ACLs and capabilities go further.
  • Treating timestamps as exact — atime updates are often disabled for performance; ctime is not creation time on Unix (it's metadata change time).
  • Building paths by string concatenation across platforms — '/' vs '' bites; use OS-aware path utilities.

Quick recap

A file is named, persistent bytes plus OS metadata. Common operations map to system calls (open, read, write, close, seek). Types include regular, directory, symlink, hardlink, device, FIFO. Paths are absolute or relative; permissions follow the Unix nine-bit model or Windows ACLs. stat exposes metadata. All higher-level file APIs build on these primitives.

Glossary

File
Named, persistent collection of bytes plus OS metadata.
Directory
Special file mapping names to file IDs (inodes).
File descriptor
Per-process integer handle returned by open; identifies the file in subsequent calls.
Hard link
Additional name for the same underlying file (inode).
Symbolic link
File whose contents is a path pointing to another file.

📖 Worked example — allocation methods, compared on one file

WORKED EXAMPLE — a 5-block file, three ways
• Contiguous: blocks 100-104. Fast sequential AND random access (address = start + i), but growth may require relocation and free space fragments externally.
• Linked: 100→250→31→77→… each block points to the next. Grows freely, zero external fragmentation — but block 4 requires walking 4 pointers (terrible random access). FAT centralizes those pointers in a table.
• Indexed (inode-style): one index block lists [100, 250, 31, 77, 501] — direct random access, easy growth; big files chain through indirect blocks (pointers to pointer blocks).
Unix inodes mix them: 12 direct pointers + single/double/triple indirect — small files stay cheap, huge files stay possible.
⚠️ MATCH METHOD TO ACCESS PATTERN
“Best random access?” contiguous/indexed. “Worst random access?” linked. “No external fragmentation?” linked/indexed. Journaling adds crash-consistency by logging metadata changes before applying them.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Beneath the familiar API of files and directories sits a careful design — inodes, blocks, free lists, journals. Each layer trades performance for reliability or vice versa. Knowing how a file system actually stores data explains its strengths, its limits, and why some operations are fast while others are surprisingly slow.

Core concepts

1. Layered structure. Top: file system API (open, read, write). Middle: file system implementation (inodes, blocks, allocation). Bottom: block device driver (read/write disk sectors). Each layer abstracts the layer below; debugging often requires reasoning down through them.

2. Inodes — the heart of Unix-style FS. An inode holds a file's metadata and pointers to its data blocks. The directory entry maps a name to an inode number. Same file can have many directory entries (hard links) all pointing to one inode. Inodes are pre-allocated; running out of inodes means 'disk full' even with bytes free.

3. Block allocation strategies. Contiguous allocation: file in one extent. Fast read, hard to grow. Linked allocation: blocks form a chain. Easy growth, slow random access. Indexed allocation: an index block lists data blocks. The hybrid winner — used by ext4, NTFS, APFS.

4. The free-block list. Track which blocks are free. Bitmap (one bit per block, scanned linearly) or free-list (linked list of free blocks). Bitmaps are compact and parallelizable; free-lists need no scan but lose locality. Modern FS use bitmaps.

5. Caching — the page cache. Recently-read blocks live in RAM. Future reads hit the cache (microseconds) instead of disk (milliseconds). Writes go to cache first (write-back) and flush later. Massive performance win; the source of 'why is read slow on first run, fast on second?'

6. Journaling for crash safety. If a crash happens mid-update, the file system can be inconsistent (allocated blocks not in any file, dirty bitmaps). Journaling: write intentions to a log first, then apply. On crash, replay the log. ext4, NTFS, APFS, ZFS all journal in some form. Trades a small write overhead for crash recovery.

7. Modern alternatives. Copy-on-write file systems (ZFS, Btrfs, APFS): every write creates a new block; old blocks remain until garbage-collected. Enables snapshots and rollback. Log-structured (F2FS for flash): writes always go to the head of a log. Each design optimizes different tradeoffs.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Running out of inodes despite free space — happens with millions of tiny files.
  • Treating write() as 'on disk now' — it's in the page cache; fsync forces flush.
  • Assuming journals make all data safe — most journals cover metadata only; data integrity needs CoW or full data journaling.
  • Comparing FS performance without specifying workload — sequential, random, small, large, read, write all matter differently.

Quick recap

File systems use inodes for metadata, blocks for data, indexed allocation for growth-friendly storage. Free-block bitmaps track availability. The page cache makes reads fast. Journaling protects metadata across crashes. Modern designs (CoW, log-structured) optimize for snapshots, flash, or specific workloads. Layering enables generic APIs over diverse implementations.

Glossary

Inode
Per-file structure holding metadata and pointers to data blocks.
Block
Fixed-size unit of disk allocation (typically 4 KB).
Indexed allocation
Block-allocation strategy using an index block listing data blocks.
Page cache
In-memory cache of file blocks; backbone of fast file I/O.
Journaling file system
FS that writes intentions to a log before applying changes, enabling crash recovery.
