📖 Worked example — disk scheduling, head movement counted

WORKED EXAMPLE — queue [98, 183, 37, 122], head at 53
• FCFS: 53→98→183→37→122 = 45+85+146+85 = 361 cylinders.
• SSTF (nearest first): 53→37→98→122→183 = 16+61+24+61 = 162.
• SCAN (elevator, moving up): 53→98→122→183 then reverse →37 = 130+146 = 276… with more requests SCAN’s one-sweep fairness beats SSTF’s starvation risk.
SSTF minimizes movement greedily but can starve far requests; SCAN/C-SCAN sweep like an elevator for bounded waiting. (For SSDs, none of this matters — no head — so schedulers mostly just merge requests.)
⚠️ COUNT MOVEMENT, NOT STOPS
These problems grade total cylinder DISTANCE. List the visit order, sum the absolute differences — arithmetic slips lose more points than concept errors here.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

On spinning disks, the order in which I/O requests are served drastically affects throughput. On SSDs, the calculus changes — but new concerns (wear, write amplification, FTL) take over. Understanding both lets you reason about why some workloads scale on storage and others don't.

Core concepts

1. The mechanics of HDD access. Moving the head (seek) is the slow part — milliseconds. Rotation latency adds another few ms. Sequential reads, where the head doesn't move, are 100x faster than random ones. The order of requests changes total time.

2. Disk scheduling algorithms — HDD era. FCFS: serve in arrival order. Seeky. SSTF: serve nearest first. Starves far requests. SCAN ('elevator'): sweep across; reverse at end. Fair, predictable. C-SCAN: only sweep one direction. More uniform. LOOK / C-LOOK: sweep only as far as outstanding requests reach.

3. SSD characteristics differ fundamentally. No moving parts. Reads are uniformly fast. Writes are slower; writes to a cell require erasing the whole erase block first. Wear: cells fail after a finite number of writes. SSDs use a Flash Translation Layer (FTL) to remap, batch, and wear-level.

4. Write amplification. One logical write may cost several physical writes — read-modify-write of an erase block, garbage collection, wear-leveling moves. SSDs measure write amplification; high values shorten lifespan. Aligned writes and TRIM commands help.

5. TRIM and the OS-SSD partnership. TRIM tells the SSD which blocks the file system no longer uses. Without it, the SSD believes everything is in use and can't garbage-collect efficiently. Modern OSes issue TRIM during deletion or as background work. Forgetting it (older OSes, some embedded) hurts SSD performance over time.

6. RAID and storage redundancy. RAID 0: striped, no redundancy, fast. RAID 1: mirrored, double space cost, redundant. RAID 5: distributed parity, one disk can fail. RAID 6: two disks. RAID 10: mirror + stripe. Modern alternatives: ZFS RAIDZ, Ceph, software-defined storage.

7. From mechanical to NVMe. SATA SSDs sit at ~500 MB/s. NVMe SSDs sit at GB/s. NVMe over Fabrics extends this across networks. The OS storage stack has been redesigned in the last decade to keep up — multi-queue block layer, polling instead of interrupts at high IOPS.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Tuning HDD-era scheduling on SSDs — 'noop' or 'mq-deadline' is usually right; SCAN-derived schedulers don't apply.
  • Forgetting TRIM on older systems — SSD performance degrades over months.
  • Treating RAID as a backup — it isn't. It protects against drive failure, not corruption, deletion, or disaster.
  • Comparing SSDs by sequential throughput when the workload is random — IOPS matter more for databases.

Quick recap

HDD scheduling is dominated by seek minimization; SCAN-family algorithms reduce average wait. SSDs have uniform read times but suffer from write amplification managed by an FTL. TRIM is essential for sustained SSD performance. RAID provides redundancy or speed. NVMe and modern OS storage stacks have removed bottlenecks that limited older designs.

Glossary

Seek time
Time for HDD head to move to a target track.
SCAN / elevator algorithm
Disk schedule sweeping across the disk in one direction.
FTL
Flash Translation Layer — SSD firmware mapping logical to physical, handling wear-leveling.
TRIM
OS-to-SSD command marking blocks as unused, enabling efficient garbage collection.
RAID
Redundant Array of Independent Disks — strategy combining drives for performance, redundancy, or both.

◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Disk and network are slow compared to CPU. The OS's I/O subsystem — drivers, buffering, scheduling, async I/O models — shapes how applications wait, batch, and overlap I/O with computation. Understanding it explains why one server handles 10x the traffic of another with identical hardware.

Core concepts

1. Device drivers as kernel modules. Each device class has a driver: disk, NIC, GPU, USB, sound. Drivers translate generic OS requests into device-specific commands. Most drivers run in kernel mode; bugs in them can crash the kernel. User-mode drivers exist (USB, FUSE file systems) for safety at slight performance cost.

2. Polling vs interrupts. Polling: CPU repeatedly checks if device is ready. Wastes cycles when device is idle. Interrupts: device signals CPU when ready. CPU does other work meanwhile. Interrupts win for slow devices. Polling wins again for very fast devices (NVMe at high IOPS) where interrupt overhead exceeds the saved waiting.

3. DMA — Direct Memory Access. Devices transfer data to and from RAM without CPU intervention. CPU sets up the transfer, device does the bulk move, CPU is interrupted on completion. Without DMA, every byte would pass through the CPU. With it, the CPU is free to do real work.

4. Buffering and double buffering. OS buffers reads and writes. Reads are typically buffered: data arrives, kernel reads ahead. Writes are typically write-back: cached, flushed later. Double-buffering: while one buffer fills, the other is processed — overlapping I/O with computation.

5. Blocking, non-blocking, and async I/O. Blocking: read() waits until data arrives. Simple. Non-blocking: returns immediately, possibly with no data. Caller polls or waits via select/poll/epoll. Async: caller submits a request and is notified on completion. Each model fits different concurrency patterns.

6. The select / poll / epoll evolution. select: wait for I/O on a fixed list of FDs (limited by FD_SETSIZE). poll: same idea, no fixed limit. epoll (Linux), kqueue (BSD), IOCP (Windows): efficient even with thousands of FDs. The progression that made high-concurrency servers (Nginx, Node.js) possible.

7. io_uring — the modern Linux interface. Submission and completion rings shared between kernel and userspace. Lock-free, batched, supports both file and socket I/O uniformly. Replaces a generation of separate APIs. Required for multi-million-IOPS NVMe workloads.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Polling when the load is low — wastes CPU; let interrupts wake you.
  • Doing I/O without DMA assumptions — copying into and out of kernel buffers can exceed the wire bandwidth.
  • Building event loops on top of select for thousands of connections — its O(n) cost dominates; use epoll/kqueue/io_uring.
  • Ignoring the difference between blocking, non-blocking, and async I/O — they need different application architectures.

Quick recap

I/O performance comes from drivers, DMA, buffering, and concurrency model. Polling vs interrupts depends on device speed. The blocking → non-blocking → async progression maps to select → epoll → io_uring. High-throughput servers stand on these primitives; understanding them is the difference between scaling smoothly and hitting a wall.

Glossary

Device driver
Kernel code translating generic OS requests into device-specific operations.
DMA
Direct Memory Access — devices read/write RAM without CPU mediation.
Polling vs interrupts
Two ways the CPU learns the device is ready: actively checking vs receiving signals.
epoll / kqueue / IOCP
Modern OS event-notification mechanisms scaling to thousands of connections.
io_uring
Recent Linux interface providing high-throughput, batched, async file and socket I/O.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — permissions & least privilege in action

WORKED EXAMPLE — decode rwxr-x--- and chmod 750
rwxr-x--- on a file owned by nat/staff:
• owner (nat): rwx = read, write, execute.
• group (staff): r-x = read + execute, no write.
• others: --- = nothing.
In octal: rwx=7, r-x=5, ---=0 → chmod 750. An access-control LIST generalizes this (per-user entries); a capability list flips the view (per-process tickets).
Least privilege: a web server runs as a low-privilege user so a compromise can’t rewrite the OS — every “why did the design do X?” security answer is some form of least privilege.
⚠️ ACL vs CAPABILITY — TWO VIEWS OF ONE MATRIX
The access matrix (subjects × objects) stored by COLUMN = ACLs (per object: who may touch me); by ROW = capabilities (per subject: what I may touch). Exams ask which is which.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Multiuser systems must isolate users from each other and from the kernel. Protection is the mechanism; access control is the policy. Understanding the models — DAC, MAC, RBAC, capabilities — and their concrete realizations (Unix permissions, ACLs, SELinux) is foundational to system security.

Core concepts

1. The protection question. Who can do what to which object? 'Who' is a subject (user, process). 'What' is an operation (read, write, execute, delete). 'Which' is an object (file, socket, process, device). Every access control model answers this triple in some way.

2. Discretionary Access Control (DAC). Owners decide who can access their resources. Unix file permissions are DAC. Flexible but error-prone — users can accidentally over-share. Default in most general-purpose OSes.

3. Mandatory Access Control (MAC). System-wide policy overrides individual users. Subjects and objects have labels (Top Secret, Secret, Confidential); the policy enforces 'no read up, no write down' (Bell-LaPadula). SELinux and AppArmor implement MAC on Linux. Used in high-security and government settings.

4. Role-Based Access Control (RBAC). Permissions assigned to roles; users assigned to roles. Easier admin than per-user permissions. Adopted everywhere — databases, cloud platforms (IAM), enterprise apps. Different from DAC/MAC because it's organizational, not OS-level, but the models compose.

5. Capability-based security. Instead of checking permissions on every access, give the subject an unforgeable token (capability) representing the right to do something specific. The token IS the permission. Used in capability OSes (KeyKOS, seL4) and modern systems like file descriptors (a kind of capability) and OAuth tokens.

6. Least privilege. Every process should have only the permissions it actually needs. setuid binaries, dropped privileges after startup, separate service accounts. The principle is older than every concrete mechanism that implements it. Violations are how exploitable bugs become catastrophic breaches.

7. Sandboxing. Restrict a process to a subset of OS capabilities — no network, limited file access, restricted syscalls. Browsers sandbox each tab. Mobile apps run sandboxed by default. seccomp on Linux, App Sandbox on macOS. The trend is more sandboxing, not less.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Running services as root because 'easier' — when compromised, root means total system access.
  • Treating Unix permissions as enough for shared-user systems — ACLs or RBAC may be needed.
  • Misconfiguring SELinux into permissive mode and forgetting to fix it — common 'works again' fix that disables protection.
  • Granting capabilities permanently when they should be temporary — once granted, hard to revoke.

Quick recap

DAC: owners control. MAC: system policy enforces labels. RBAC: roles bundle permissions. Capabilities: unforgeable tokens grant specific rights. Least privilege limits any one component's blast radius. Sandboxing constrains processes to a subset of OS capabilities. Real systems combine these; defense in depth is the goal.

Glossary

DAC
Discretionary Access Control — owners set permissions.
MAC
Mandatory Access Control — system-wide policy overrides users.
RBAC
Role-Based Access Control — permissions via roles.
Capability
Unforgeable token representing a specific right.
Least privilege
Principle: each component has only the permissions it actually needs.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — how login actually checks your password

WORKED EXAMPLE — salted hashing, end to end
At signup: system generates a random salt, computes hash(salt + password), stores salt + hash — NEVER the password.
At login: recompute hash(stored salt + typed password); match → in.
Why the salt? Two users with the same password get DIFFERENT hashes, and precomputed rainbow tables become useless — each guess must be re-hashed per salt.

MFA stacks factors: something you know (password) + have (phone code) + are (fingerprint) — stealing one factor no longer suffices. Encryption’s role: symmetric (one shared key, fast, AES) for data, asymmetric (public/private, RSA) for key exchange and signatures.
⚠️ HASHING ≠ ENCRYPTION
Encryption is reversible with the key; hashing is deliberately ONE-WAY. Passwords are hashed (nobody, including the OS, should recover them) — saying “passwords are encrypted” is the answer graders mark wrong.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Authentication is how the system verifies who you are. Cryptography is the math that makes proofs possible across untrusted networks. Both rely on building blocks — passwords, keys, hashes, certificates — that the OS exposes through APIs. Misuse is how breaches happen.

Core concepts

1. Authentication factors. Something you know (password). Something you have (phone, hardware key). Something you are (fingerprint, face). Multi-factor combines categories. Modern thinking: password alone is not enough; at least two factors for anything sensitive.

2. Password storage — never plain. Always hash, never store plaintext. The hash should be slow on purpose: bcrypt, scrypt, argon2, PBKDF2. Per-user salt prevents rainbow-table attacks. SHA-256 alone is wrong — too fast, no salt by default. Frameworks provide the right primitives.

3. Symmetric encryption. Same key encrypts and decrypts. AES-256 is the workhorse. Modes (CBC, GCM, CTR) determine guarantees. AES-GCM is the standard recommendation — confidentiality plus authenticated integrity. Key management is harder than the math.

4. Asymmetric encryption. Public/private key pairs. Anyone can encrypt with the public key; only the holder of the private key can decrypt. RSA, ECC. Slower than symmetric, so usually used to wrap a symmetric session key. The basis of TLS, SSH, signing.

5. Hashes and digital signatures. Cryptographic hash (SHA-256, BLAKE3) summarizes any input to a fixed-size value. Signing: encrypt the hash with your private key; anyone can verify with your public key. The basis of code signing, TLS certificates, blockchain.

6. TLS — what protects most network traffic. Three-step handshake: agree on parameters, exchange keys (often using public key to wrap a symmetric session key), authenticate server (and optionally client) via certificates. After handshake, all traffic is symmetrically encrypted. The shape of HTTPS, IMAPS, SSH.

7. Certificate authorities and trust. Public-key infrastructure (PKI): a hierarchy of certificate authorities (CAs) signs server certificates. Browsers and OSes ship with a list of trusted root CAs. Compromised or rogue CAs are a real and recurring threat; certificate transparency logs help mitigate.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Storing passwords as plain text — the foundational mistake that recurs in breach after breach.
  • Using fast hashes (MD5, SHA-1, SHA-256) for password storage — they're built for speed; you want slowness.
  • Building your own crypto — almost always wrong; use vetted libraries (libsodium, OpenSSL, BoringSSL, AWS KMS).
  • Trusting any certificate the system presents without checking the chain or expiration.

Quick recap

Authentication uses something you know, have, or are; multi-factor combines them. Passwords must be hashed with slow, salted algorithms. Symmetric encryption (AES-GCM) is fast; asymmetric (RSA, ECC) handles key exchange and signing. TLS protects most network traffic via handshake-then-symmetric. PKI manages identity through certificate authorities. Use vetted libraries; never roll your own.

Glossary

Multi-factor authentication
Authentication using two or more independent factors.
Salt
Per-user random value combined with password before hashing to defeat rainbow tables.
AES-GCM
Symmetric cipher providing both encryption and authentication (integrity).
Public-key cryptography
Schemes using paired keys (public for encrypt/verify, private for decrypt/sign).
TLS
Transport Layer Security — protocol securing most modern network traffic via handshake then symmetric encryption.

📊 FIGURE — the key terms of this section

📖 Worked example — name the attack from the symptom

WORKED EXAMPLE — four incidents, classified
• A program writes past a fixed-size input array and overwrites the return address → buffer overflow (defenses: bounds checking, stack canaries, ASLR, non-executable stacks).
• An email “from IT” asks for your password → phishing / social engineering (defense: training + MFA).
• A program disguised as a free game opens a backdoor → Trojan horse; self-replicating over the network without a host program → worm; attaching to other executables → virus.
• Thousands of machines flood a server with traffic → DDoS (defense: filtering, rate limits, CDNs).
Defense-in-depth: no single wall — permissions + patching + MFA + monitoring stacked.
⚠️ WORM vs VIRUS vs TROJAN
Worm spreads ITSELF over the network; virus attaches to a host program and needs it run; trojan pretends to be legitimate and doesn’t self-replicate. Three definitions, endlessly swapped in options.
◆ WHY THIS MATTERS

Every OS faces real attackers, and every defense fits somewhere on a spectrum from prevention to detection to recovery. Knowing the canonical threats — buffer overflows, privilege escalation, malware, social engineering — and the defenses against each is the working vocabulary of OS security.

Core concepts

1. The CIA triad. Confidentiality (data not exposed). Integrity (data not tampered). Availability (system reachable when needed). Every threat targets one or more; every defense protects one or more. Naming the dimension clarifies design choices.

2. Buffer overflows and memory corruption. Writing past array bounds overwrites adjacent memory — sometimes the return address, sometimes a function pointer. Classic exploit primitive. Defenses: stack canaries, ASLR (randomized memory layout), DEP/NX (non-executable data pages), bounds checking in safe languages.

3. Privilege escalation. An attacker gains higher privileges than authorized — local user becomes root, web server breaks out of sandbox. Often combines a small bug (memory corruption) with access to a privileged target (setuid binary, kernel syscall). Defenses: least privilege, sandboxing, kernel hardening (KASLR, kPTI).

4. Malware categories. Virus: attaches to files, propagates with execution. Worm: self-propagates over network. Trojan: looks legitimate, hides malicious code. Ransomware: encrypts data, demands payment. Rootkit: hides itself in the kernel. Each requires different detection and response.

5. Social engineering and phishing. Bypassing technical defenses by attacking humans. Phishing emails, fake login pages, pretexting calls. Often the easiest entry point. Defenses: user training, MFA (especially hardware keys), email filtering. Technical hardening alone leaves a large open door.

6. Defense in depth. No single layer is enough. Network firewalls + host firewalls + segmentation + endpoint hardening + monitoring + IR. An attacker breaching one layer should hit another. Even an obvious vuln is less catastrophic when surrounded by other controls.

7. Detection, response, and recovery. Prevention fails sometimes; detection matters too. SIEM and EDR systems collect telemetry; humans investigate alerts. Incident response: contain, eradicate, recover, learn. Backups (offline, immutable) are the last line against ransomware. Tabletop exercises beat theoretical readiness.

⚠ COMMON PITFALLS
  • Treating perimeter defense as enough — once an attacker is inside, the inside is often soft.
  • Disabling protective measures (ASLR, SELinux, secure boot) for convenience — common cause of incidents.
  • Backups that are accessible from production — ransomware encrypts those too. Offline / immutable backups matter.
  • Focusing only on technical defenses while users can be socially engineered — humans are the most exploited surface.

Quick recap

Threats target confidentiality, integrity, or availability. Buffer overflows, privilege escalation, malware, and social engineering are the canonical categories. Defenses include memory-safety mitigations (canaries, ASLR, DEP), least privilege, sandboxing, MFA, defense in depth, and detection / response / recovery. Backups must be offline. Humans are part of the threat model.

Glossary

CIA triad
Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability — three goals security protects.
Buffer overflow
Writing past array bounds; classic exploit primitive in unsafe languages.
ASLR / DEP
Address Space Layout Randomization / Data Execution Prevention — memory-safety mitigations.
Privilege escalation
Attack gaining higher privileges than the attacker should have.
Defense in depth
Layered security — no single layer is the only protection.

Virus: self-replicates by attaching to files/programs and spreading when they run. SQL injection: attacker-supplied input injects database commands — defeated by parameterized queries. XSS (cross-site scripting): injecting malicious scripts into pages other users view — defeated by output encoding. DoS (denial of service): flooding a system to destroy availability — the attack aims at the A in CIA.

📖 Worked example — attacking this course’s assessment tasks

WORKED EXAMPLE — an OS scenario task, decomposed
Tasks in OS courses are scenario analyses: “Given workload X, choose and justify a scheduling algorithm / memory strategy.” The winning pattern:

1. Extract the workload facts — interactive vs batch? long vs short jobs? memory-constrained?
2. Name the candidates with one-line trade-offs (RR: responsive, overhead; SJF: optimal wait, starvation…).
3. Choose and JUSTIFY with the scenario’s facts — “because the workload is interactive, bounded response time matters more than minimal average wait, so round-robin with a moderate quantum…”
4. Show the mechanics — a small worked timeline/computation proving you can apply, not just name, the choice.
The justification carries the points; a correct pick with no scenario-tied reasoning rates Approaching.

The deliverable in one breath

D686 Operating Systems for Computer Scientists has two graded components: a proctored, multiple-choice objective assessment (OA) covering OS fundamentals, and this performance task (PA). This playbook is only for the PA. The OA is studied separately — practice recall of definitions and the mechanics of the algorithms below, because the OA rewards speed and precision while the PA rewards applied reasoning.

The PA is a written technical analysis / applied task. You are handed a scenario (often a company, server, or application with performance, concurrency, or resource problems) and asked to analyze it through core OS concepts, then justify recommendations. Exact wording and lettering change over time, so confirm the current task prompt and rubric in your course — but the concept coverage is stable.

The four concept pillars

  • Process & thread management and CPU scheduling — explain processes vs. threads and context switching; compare FCFS, SJF (and SRTF), Round-Robin, and priority scheduling; compute waiting time and turnaround time for a given burst set and recommend a policy for the scenario's workload.
  • Synchronization & deadlock — identify race conditions on shared data; apply mutex/semaphore (and monitors) to protect critical sections; state the four Coffman conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait); distinguish deadlock prevention, avoidance (Banker's algorithm), detection, and recovery.
  • Memory management — explain paging, segmentation, and virtual memory (page tables, TLB, demand paging); trace page-replacement algorithms FIFO, LRU, and Optimal (OPT) for a reference string and count page faults; discuss thrashing and working sets.
  • File systems & security — file allocation methods, directory structures, and access control / permissions relevant to the scenario.

The single most important framing: every section must tie back to the scenario. Evaluators want to see the concept, the computation or mechanism, and then a justified recommendation for this workload — not a textbook paragraph that could apply to any system.

📖 Worked example — pre-submit sweep for scenario answers

WORKED EXAMPLE — a returned answer, fixed
Case: returned on “justifies the selection” — the student picked LRU and defined it correctly, but never said why it fits THE GIVEN workload.
Fix: one paragraph tying the choice to the scenario’s stated locality (“the trace re-uses recent pages heavily, which is exactly the pattern LRU exploits; FIFO would evict the hot pages because…”) — plus a 5-line fault-count comparison as evidence.

The sweep: every requirement verb has a labeled section; every choice has a scenario-tied justification; every computation shows its steps (graders award the METHOD); terminology exact (page vs frame, deadlock vs starvation); counts and formats match the task sheet.

Pre-submission checklist

  1. Scenario tie-in per section. Read each paragraph and ask: could this apply to any system? If yes, add the scenario's specifics.
  2. Re-verify all math. Recompute every Gantt chart, waiting/turnaround average, and page-fault count independently. Arithmetic slips are a top return reason.
  3. Coffman conditions listed exactly: mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait.
  4. Prevention vs. avoidance kept straight. Prevention = design so one Coffman condition can never hold. Avoidance = allow the conditions but use runtime state (Banker's algorithm) to only grant requests that leave the system in a safe state.
  5. Page-replacement traces shown frame-by-frame for FIFO, LRU, and Optimal, with the fault count under each.
  6. Every recommendation has a justification clause ("...because the workload is X").
  7. Headings mirror the rubric so evaluators find each aspect fast.
  8. Proofread for terminology and citations.

Why PAs get returned

  • Generic descriptions. Explaining Round-Robin in the abstract without applying it to the scenario's processes. Fix: always compute and recommend for the given data.
  • Arithmetic errors. A wrong turnaround average or miscounted page fault fails the aspect even if the method is right. Fix: recompute from scratch and sanity-check (e.g., Optimal should never fault more than LRU or FIFO on the same string).
  • Confusing deadlock prevention with avoidance. Fix: prevention breaks a Coffman condition by design; avoidance uses Banker's to check safe states dynamically — detection/recovery act after deadlock occurs.
  • Recommendations without justification. Fix: end every recommendation with "because..." grounded in the scenario.
Quick sanity check: for the same reference string and frame count, Optimal ≤ LRU and Optimal ≤ FIFO in faults; and increasing frames should not increase LRU/Optimal faults. If your numbers violate this, recheck the trace (FIFO can show Belady's anomaly, so it is the exception).

📖 Worked example — a hard scheduling + sync problem

WORKED EXAMPLE — priority inversion, diagnosed
Low-priority L holds a lock. High-priority H blocks waiting for it. Medium-priority M (no lock involvement) preempts L — so M runs while H starves: priority inversion (the Mars Pathfinder bug).

Fix: priority inheritance — while L holds a lock H wants, L temporarily runs at H’s priority, finishes the critical section, releases, and priorities snap back. M can no longer wedge between them.
Recognize the pattern: “high waits on low, medium runs” → inversion; the cure is inheritance (or priority ceilings).

Turning a burst table into a number

Every scheduling metric reduces to three quantities per process. Completion time is when the process finishes on the Gantt chart. Turnaround = completion - arrival. Waiting = turnaround - burst (equivalently, time spent in the ready queue). Average waiting time is the mean of the per-process waiting times. The only hard part is building the Gantt chart correctly.

Algorithm mechanics

  • FCFS: run in arrival order; simple but suffers the convoy effect when a long job blocks short ones.
  • SJF (non-preemptive): at each dispatch, among arrived jobs pick the smallest remaining burst; it runs to completion.
  • SRTF (preemptive SJF): re-evaluate on every arrival; a newly arrived job with a shorter remaining time preempts the running job. SRTF is provably optimal for average waiting time.
  • Round-Robin: each job gets one quantum, then goes to the tail of the ready queue; a preempted job re-enters behind jobs that arrived during its slice.
  • Priority: dispatch the highest priority (here, lowest number); starvation is the classic hazard, aging is the cure.

Deadlock and synchronization

Deadlock needs all four Coffman conditions simultaneously: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Prevention removes one condition; the Banker's algorithm instead avoids unsafe states by granting a request only if a safe sequence still exists. A safe sequence is any ordering in which each process's Need can be met by the current Available plus the resources freed by earlier finishers. For semaphores, track the integer directly: wait() decrements, signal() increments, and a counting semaphore's value equals free resource units. Race conditions arise whenever a read-modify-write on shared state (like count++) is interleaved without a lock.

"},"D686/challenge/c2":{"body":"

📖 Worked example — a hard memory-performance problem

WORKED EXAMPLE — effective access time with page faults
Memory access 100 ns; page fault service 8 ms; fault rate p.
EAT = (1 − p) × 100ns + p × 8,000,000ns.
At p = 0.001 (one fault per thousand!): EAT = 99.9 + 8000 = 8,100 ns — 81× slower than RAM.
To keep degradation under 10% (110 ns): p × 8ms ≤ 10ns → p ≤ 1.25 × 10⁻⁶ — about one fault per 800,000 accesses.
Moral (and the exam answer): disk is SO slow that page faults must be astronomically rare; locality and enough RAM are everything.

From logical address to a real byte

Split any logical address into a page number and an offset. With page size S, page number = address div S and offset = address mod S. The page table maps the page number to a frame number; the physical address is frame * S + offset. The offset never changes during translation, only the high-order bits do.

Making translation fast

A TLB caches recent page-table entries. Effective access time weights the hit and miss paths: on a hit you pay the TLB lookup plus one memory reference; on a miss you pay the TLB lookup, a memory reference to read the page table, and a second memory reference for the data. EAT = hit_ratio x (t_TLB + t_mem) + miss_ratio x (t_TLB + 2 x t_mem).

Page replacement

For a reference string and a fixed frame count, count faults by simulating each policy. FIFO evicts the oldest-loaded page and can suffer Belady's anomaly, where adding frames increases faults. LRU evicts the least-recently-used page; Optimal (OPT) evicts the page used farthest in the future and gives the theoretical minimum. LRU and OPT are stack algorithms, so they never exhibit Belady's anomaly. A process's working set is the set of distinct pages referenced in the last Delta references; if the sum of working sets exceeds available frames, the system thrashes.

Disk and files

Seek distance is the total head movement summed over the service order (FCFS, SSTF, SCAN). For file size, an inode's block pointers form a tree: a single-indirect block holds (block_size / pointer_size) pointers, a double-indirect block squares that fan-out, and a triple-indirect cubes it, each pointer ultimately naming one data block.

🧠 The Aistote Method (J-Method)

THE IDEA
The Aistote app is built on two of the most evidence-backed study techniques — active recall and spaced repetition — run in short, intense 25-minute blocks (its "J-Method"). Instead of slowly re-reading, you spend the time testing yourself and re-testing what you miss. This app already has every tool the method needs.
THE 3-STEP LOOP
StepWhat you doWhere in this app
1. ConvertTurn the material into questions instead of re-reading it.Open a section, skim the lesson once, then jump to its Quiz.
2. RecallAnswer from memory first — no peeking — then check.Take the section Quiz, or a PA / OA simulation; rate your confidence.
3. Space itRe-test only what you missed, on a growing schedule.Every miss becomes a Flashcard; review them on the app's spaced-repetition schedule.
A 25-MINUTE J-METHOD SESSION
TimeDo this
0–3 minSkim the lesson's key terms and the big idea — don't memorize yet, just get the lay of the land.
3–18 minTake the section quiz (or a 15-question drill). Try to recall the answer first, reveal it after.
18–23 minRedo only the questions you got wrong.
23–25 minSend the stubborn ones to Flashcards and note tomorrow's quick review.
Start the block with the ⚡ Focus timer (25 min) on any lesson — that is your J-Method session.
⚠️ THE ONE RULE
Always try to answer from memory before you look. The effort of retrieving is what actually builds the memory — re-reading feels productive but barely moves it.
WHY IT WORKS
Active recall (testing yourself) forces your brain to reconstruct the answer, which strengthens it far more than recognition. Spaced repetition reviews each fact just as you're about to forget it, moving it into long-term memory with the fewest reps. The 25-minute block simply makes you actually do both, every day.
DAILY RHYTHM
Two or three 25-minute J-Method blocks a day (new material in one, missed-question review in the next) beats a single long cram session — and it's how the Aistote method delivers "learn it in 25 minutes" instead of hours.
